notes.meaning: The Lord spoke these commands to Moses while the Israelites were still camped around Mount Sinai. This setting reminded the people that these laws came directly from God before they ever entered their new home. It joins these upcoming rules for the land with the rest of the sacred laws God delivered on the mountain.

God looked forward to the day when the people would finally settle in the Promised Land. Even the soil itself was commanded to observe a Sabbath rest dedicated to the Lord. This showed the Israelites that God was the real owner of the land and they were merely tenants enjoying His goodness.

The people were allowed to plant fields, prune grapevines, and gather their crops for six years in a row. Normal farming was a good and necessary part of their daily life. Just like the six regular workdays that led up to the weekly Sabbath, these six years set the pattern before a year of rest.

When the seventh year arrived, all farming was ordered to stop so the land could enjoy a complete Sabbath of rest to the Lord. No one was allowed to plant seeds in the fields or trim the vines in the vineyards. This pause taught the people that their food came from God's blessing rather than their own constant toil.

Grain that sprouted on its own from seeds dropped during the previous harvest was not to be reaped into barns. Grapes that grew on unpruned vines were also left alone instead of being harvested for profit. Leaving the vines untrimmed treated them as set apart for God while the ground enjoyed a full year of rest.

Whatever food grew by itself during the Sabbath year was available for everyone to eat straight from the fields. Landowners, servants, day laborers, and visiting foreigners all shared the produce equally with farm animals and wildlife. No one was permitted to store crops away for private wealth, which taught the community charity and dependence on God.

Israel was instructed to count seven cycles of seven years, adding up to forty-nine years in total. This calendar of Sabbath years built a long rhythm of rest into the life of the whole nation. It prepared the people for an even greater celebration that arrived right after the forty-ninth year.

A loud horn was blown across the entire nation on the Day of Atonement, the tenth day of the seventh month. This was the annual day when Israel received cleansing and forgiveness for their sins. Announcing freedom right after sins were forgiven showed that true liberty and joy always flow from peace with God.

The fiftieth year was set apart as holy, and liberty was announced to all Israelites throughout the land. Any family land that had been sold reverted back to its original owner, and any servant returned home to his family. This special Jubilee prevented families from sinking into permanent poverty and protected the tribal inheritance of each clan.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that this release applied specifically to Israelites rather than abolishing foreign slavery, and they suggest the autumn trumpet blast announced a fiftieth year beginning the following spring.

notes.meaning: The fiftieth year was celebrated as a Jubilee, meaning the people did not sow seed or store up crops in barns. Families ate only what the ground produced on its own, gathering food directly from the fields each day. This extended rest was a strong test of faith that trained the people to live on God's provision rather than their own stockpiles.

In the Year of Jubilee, every Israelite returned to his original family property. This rule kept wealthy buyers from buying up all the land forever and ensured that each tribe's ancient territory stayed intact. Christian teachers have also seen this as a picture of believers being brought back to their true heavenly home through Christ.

God commanded buyers and sellers never to cheat or take unfair advantage of one another. Sellers were not allowed to overcharge, and buyers could not exploit a neighbor's poverty or lack of knowledge. Treating others fairly in business was an essential way the Israelites showed respect for God's law.

The selling price of land was calculated based strictly on the number of harvest years left before the next Jubilee. If many harvest years remained, the price was higher; if only a few years remained, the price dropped. Buyers were not purchasing the land permanently, but only buying the right to a set number of future crops.

The warning against taking advantage of neighbors is repeated along with a call to fear God. The people were reminded that the Lord sees every business deal and defends those who are cheated. Revering God in the heart naturally stops someone from doing wrong to others in word or deed.

God promised that if the people kept His statutes and lived by His rules, they would dwell safely in the land. The ground would yield abundant fruit so they could eat their fill without fear of famine or enemies. True peace and security did not come from military power, but from trusting and obeying the Lord.

God addressed the natural question the people would ask about what they would eat during the seventh year without planting or harvesting. Setting aside an entire year of farming could easily make a family worry about starvation. God brought up their honest fear so He could reassure them with a divine promise.

God promised a miraculous blessing on the sixth year's harvest so that it would produce enough food for three years. This extra supply would feed the people during the Sabbath year and sustain them while new crops grew in the eighth year, until the ninth year's harvest arrived. Just as God once gave a double portion of manna before the weekly Sabbath, He showed He could fully provide for those who rested in obedience.

Land could never be sold away permanently because the entire country belonged to God. The Israelites were only guests and temporary residents living on God's property by His grace. Remembering they were just tenants reminded them not to cling too tightly to earthly wealth, but to look forward to their eternal home with God.

Every land sale was required to include the right of redemption, which meant the seller always had a lawful way to buy the property back. No sale was final or beyond recovery. God made sure that families were never permanently stripped of the land He had assigned to them.

If an Israelite became poor and was forced to sell family land, his nearest relative had the legal right to step forward and buy it back. This close relative was called a redeemer. Commentators have long seen this kinsman redeemer as a picture of Jesus Christ, who became human in order to buy back the spiritual inheritance lost by our sin.

If a man had no relative to help him, but later earned enough money on his own, he was permitted to buy his land back. He calculated the value of the harvests since the sale and refunded only the fair balance for the years remaining until the Jubilee. Once that balance was paid, he returned immediately to his family property.

If the poor man could never gather enough money to buy back his land, the property remained with the buyer until the Year of Jubilee. When that fiftieth year arrived, the land was released freely without any money being paid. This pointed forward to God's free grace in Christ, which restores believers to God's favor without any price or human merit.
